youtube.baslik: Turkish Speech Sounds: Vowels and Consonants | Lesson 74 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In this lesson we look at the speech sounds of Turkish: the features of its eight vowels and vowel harmony, and how consonants are classified by place, manner and voicing. We also discuss which sounds are confused in hearing loss, why, and how to use this in the clinic.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Göksel A, Kerslake C (2005), Turkish: A Comprehensive Grammar, Routledge; Zimmer K, Orgun O (1999), Turkish, Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press; Miller GA, Nicely PE (1955), An analysis of perceptual confusions among some English consonants, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Vowels, consonants and confusions in hearing loss
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will get to know the speech sounds of Turkish, its vowels and consonants, through an audiologist's eyes.
We will see vowel features and vowel harmony, consonant place and manner, and which sounds are confused in hearing loss.
The smallest unit among speech sounds that changes meaning is called a phoneme.

cumleler.yazi: In Turkish, kar, snow, and gar, station, differ only in the first sound, so k and g are separate phonemes.
cumleler.ses: In Turkish, kar, snow, and gar, station, differ only in the first sound, so K and G are separate phonemes.

cumleler: The Turkish alphabet has twenty nine letters: eight vowels and twenty one consonants.

cumleler.yazi: But some letters sound different by context; for example, the l sounds in kol, arm, and göl, lake, are not the same.
cumleler.ses: But some letters sound different by context; for example, the L sounds in the Turkish words for arm and lake are not the same.

cumleler.yazi: K, g and l move toward the front of the palate next to front vowels and stay further back next to back vowels.
cumleler.ses: K, G and L move toward the front of the palate next to front vowels and stay further back next to back vowels.

cumleler.yazi: The soft g, ğ, is not heard on its own for most speakers and lengthens the preceding vowel, as in dağ, mountain.
cumleler.ses: The soft G is not heard on its own for most speakers and lengthens the preceding vowel, as in dah, mountain.

ogeler.metin: Is the tongue back or front?

cumleler: A vowel is a sound made as air leaves the mouth without obstruction; Turkish has eight vowels.
The first feature is tongue position: if the tongue is back, it is a back vowel; if it is forward, a front vowel.
The second feature is lip shape: if the lips are rounded, the vowel is rounded; if not, it is unrounded.
The third feature is mouth opening: a more open mouth gives an open vowel, and a more closed mouth a close vowel.
Each of the eight vowels is a different combination of these three features, so the Turkish vowel system is very regular.

cumleler.yazi: The back vowels are a, ı, o and u.
cumleler.ses: The back vowels are A, dotless I, O and U.

cumleler.yazi: The front vowels are e, i, ö and ü.
cumleler.ses: The front vowels are E, I, O umlaut and U umlaut.

cumleler.yazi: The unrounded vowels are a, e, ı and i; the rounded vowels are o, ö, u and ü.
cumleler.ses: The unrounded vowels are A, E, dotless I and I; the rounded vowels are O, O umlaut, U and U umlaut.

cumleler: In rounded vowels the lips are pushed forward and rounded, which clearly changes the color of the sound.

cumleler.yazi: The open vowels are a, e, o and ö.
cumleler.ses: The open vowels are A, E, O and O umlaut.

cumleler.yazi: The close vowels are ı, i, u and ü.
cumleler.ses: The close vowels are dotless I, I, U and U umlaut.

cumleler: The acoustic cues that tell vowels apart are bands of concentrated energy called formants.
The first formant is linked to mouth opening: it is higher in open vowels and lower in close vowels.
The second formant is linked to tongue position: it is high in front vowels and low in back vowels.
Rounding the lips pulls the formants down somewhat.

cumleler.yazi: So telling apart front vowels such as i and ü depends on hearing the high-frequency region that carries the second formant.
cumleler.ses: So telling apart front vowels such as ee and its rounded pair depends on hearing the high-frequency region that carries the second formant.

maddeler.metin: Major harmony: _back with back_, front with front

cumleler: An important feature of Turkish is vowel harmony.
Under major vowel harmony, a back vowel in a word is followed by back vowels, and a front vowel by front vowels.

cumleler.yazi: Suffixes change shape to match: the plural is lar in çocuklar, children, and ler in evler, houses.
cumleler.ses: Suffixes change shape to match: the plural is lar in cho-jook-lar, children, and ler in evler, houses.

cumleler: Minor vowel harmony governs how vowels follow each other in terms of rounding.

cumleler.yazi: For example, the question particle becomes mü after gözü, his eye, and mu after kolu, his arm.
cumleler.ses: For example, the question particle takes a front rounded vowel after the word for his eye, and becomes mu after kolu, his arm.

cumleler: Some loanwords such as kitap, book, and kalem, pen, break this rule; even so, suffixes are mostly chosen by the last vowel.
A consonant is a sound made as air meets an obstruction in the mouth or throat.
First, we classify consonants by place of articulation, that is, where the airflow is narrowed.
Second, we classify them by manner of articulation, that is, how the airflow is blocked.
The third dimension is voicing: if the vocal folds vibrate, the consonant is voiced; if not, it is voiceless.
These three dimensions are also the key to understanding which sounds are confused in hearing loss, and why.

cumleler.yazi: P, b and m are made by bringing both lips together.
F and v are made by bringing the lower lip close to the upper teeth.
T, d and n are made with the tongue tip touching behind the upper teeth.
S, z, l and r are made by a narrowing between the tongue tip and the area near the gum ridge.
In Turkish spelling, ş, j, ç and c stand for sh, zh, ch and j; they are made just behind the gum ridge, and y on the palate.
cumleler.ses: The sounds sh, zh, ch and j are made just behind the gum ridge, and the Y sound on the hard palate.

cumleler.yazi: K and g are made with the back of the tongue, and h in the larynx; this classification varies slightly between sources.

ogeler.metin: p, b, t, d, k, g
f, v, s, z, ş, j

cumleler.yazi: In stops, the airflow is fully closed and then suddenly released: p, b, t, d, k and g.
In fricatives, air passes with friction through a narrow gap: f, v, s, z, ş, j, and h in the larynx.
cumleler.ses: In fricatives, air passes with friction through a narrow gap: f, v, s, z, sh, zh, and h in the larynx.

cumleler.yazi: Ç and c start with a closure followed by friction; they are called affricates.
cumleler.ses: The ch and j sounds start with a closure followed by friction; they are called affricates.

cumleler.yazi: M and n are nasal sounds; the air leaves through the nose.
L and r are liquids; like vowels, they carry stronger and more continuous energy.
Y is the consonant closest to a vowel and is called a glide, or semivowel.

cumleler: Many fricatives carry weak, high-frequency energy, so they are among the first sounds lost in hearing loss.

maddeler.metin: Seven pairs: b and p, _d and t_

ogeler.metin: b and p, v and f
d and t, z and s
c and ç, j and ş

cumleler: In voiced consonants the vocal folds vibrate; in voiceless consonants they do not.

cumleler.yazi: Turkish schools teach the eight voiceless consonants with the phrase Fıstıkçı Şahap: f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h and p.
cumleler.ses: Turkish schools teach the eight voiceless consonants with the phrase Fustukchu Shahap: f, s, t, k, ch, sh, h and p.

cumleler.yazi: Most voiceless consonants have a voiced partner: b and p, c and ç, d and t, g and k, v and f, z and s, j and ş.
cumleler.ses: Most voiceless consonants have a voiced partner: b and p, j and ch, d and t, g and k, v and f, z and s, zh and sh.

cumleler.yazi: Suffixes follow this too: ç in kitapçı, bookseller, but c in gözcü, lookout; this is called consonant assimilation.
cumleler.ses: Suffixes follow this too: after a voiceless sound the suffix starts with ch, after a voiced sound with j; this is called consonant assimilation.

cumleler: In stops, an important cue for voicing is the time between the release burst and the start of vocal fold vibration.
This interval is called voice onset time, and it is largely a temporal cue.
Besides individual sounds, speech has suprasegmental features such as stress, intonation and duration.
In Turkish, word stress usually falls on the last syllable, but in place names such as Ankara and some other words it comes earlier.
Intonation, for example, separates a question from a statement and is carried largely by changes in the fundamental frequency.
The fundamental frequency and strong lower harmonics lie in the low frequencies, so intonation cues survive high-frequency loss.
So a person with high-frequency loss hears the rhythm and melody of speech but misses the details of the sounds.
In children with severe loss, the intonation and voice quality of speech may be affected because they cannot monitor their own voice.
To understand which sounds are confused in a hearing loss, let us recall the speech banana.
In this example, the loss drops above one thousand hertz; the vowels and low-frequency consonants stay above threshold.

cumleler.yazi: In contrast, many weak, high-frequency consonants such as s, ş, f and t fall below threshold.
cumleler.ses: In contrast, many weak, high-frequency consonants such as s, sh, f and t fall below threshold.

cumleler.yazi: The classic study by Miller and Nicely, published in nineteen fifty five, shows which cues are preserved in this situation.

cumleler: In noise, and when high frequencies are filtered out, voicing and nasality cues are largely preserved.
The place cue is lost most easily, because this information is carried largely in the high frequencies and in short transitions.

cumleler.yazi: S and ş are both voiceless fricatives; the only difference is place, and this difference is carried in the high frequencies.
cumleler.ses: S and sh are both voiceless fricatives; the only difference is place, and this difference is carried in the high frequencies.

cumleler.yazi: Weak fricatives such as f and s are confused with each other and may not be heard at all in high-frequency loss.
P, t and k are voiceless stops; with high-frequency loss, the person hears the burst but may confuse its place.
M and n are nasals; even if nasality is preserved, the place difference between them may be missed.
Front vowels such as i and ü may also be confused by some people, because the second formant is carried in the high frequencies.
cumleler.ses: Front vowels such as ee and its rounded pair may also be confused by some people, because the second formant is carried in the high frequencies.

cumleler: In contrast, pairs such as b and p, which differ only in voicing, are told apart relatively well in high-frequency loss.

sahneler.metin: In word tests, note the error type, not just the percent correct: was place, manner or voicing missed? This guides fitting and training.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: in a word recognition test, do not settle for recording only the percent correct.
For words repeated wrongly, note which sound was confused with which.
If most errors are place confusions, high-frequency audibility may be insufficient; this guides the hearing aid fitting.
The same error analysis also decides which sound pairs to work on in auditory training.

maddeler.metin: High-frequency loss: the _place_ cue is lost

cumleler: The eight Turkish vowels are classified by three features: back or front, unrounded or rounded, and open or close.
Vowel harmony makes the vowels in words and suffixes match each other.
Consonants are defined by place of articulation, manner of articulation and voicing.
In high-frequency hearing loss, voicing and nasality are better preserved; the cue lost most easily is place of articulation.

sahneler.soru: Which consonant cue is lost most easily in high-frequency loss?
sahneler.aciklama: Place information is carried largely in the _high frequencies_ and in short formant transitions.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a person with high-frequency hearing loss, which consonant cue is lost most easily?
The correct answer is C: place of articulation.

cumleler: Place is carried in the high frequencies and short transitions, while voicing and nasality survive in the low frequencies too.
